client: I've been really struggling since my mom passed away six months ago. It happened so suddenly, and I feel like everyone around me has just... moved on, like they've gone back to their normal lives, while I'm still stuck in this fog. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I guess I'm here because I don't know what else to do.
therapist: I'm so glad you're here, and I want you to know that what you're carrying — this grief, this sense of being left behind in the fog while the world moves on — is one of the most isolating feelings a person can experience, and it makes complete sense given how sudden and profound your loss was. There's no timeline for grief, and the fact that others seem to have "moved on" doesn't mean your pain is wrong or too much — it just means they may not fully see what you're still living through. I also hear your doubt about whether talking will help, and I think that's worth honoring rather than pushing past — so I'm curious, what does a day in that fog actually feel like for you?

client: A typical day feels like I'm moving through everything on autopilot — I go to work, I answer emails, I make dinner — but none of it feels real, like I'm watching myself from a distance. I'll be fine for a few hours and then something small will happen, like seeing a brand of tea she used to drink, and it just... hits me all over again and I can't function. The worst part is I feel guilty even having okay moments, like if I'm not actively sad then I'm somehow forgetting her or not grieving her the right way.
therapist: What you're describing — that dissociated, autopilot feeling alongside those sudden waves of grief — is actually a very common and real part of loss, not a sign that something is wrong with you. And that guilt about the okay moments is so worth gently examining, because there's a thought hiding in there that says "feeling okay = forgetting her," and I wonder if we could look at whether that's actually true — can you think of anyone you love deeply right now, in this moment, even while not actively feeling sad about them? What do you notice when you sit with that?

client: I see what you're doing there, and I guess... yeah, I love my brother, and I'm not sitting here crying about him right now, but that doesn't mean I love him any less. But it still feels different somehow with my mom, like the stakes are higher because she's gone and I can't ever show her again that I love her, so the okay moments feel like a betrayal in a way I can't quite explain. I don't know if that logic holds up, but it's hard to just think my way out of a feeling, you know?
therapist: You just articulated something really profound — that the guilt isn't really about forgetting her, it's about the permanence, the fact that the relationship feels frozen in time and the okay moments can't be "balanced out" by showing her your love again, and that's a genuinely different kind of pain that deserves to be understood, not just reasoned away. You're absolutely right that we can't think our way out of feelings, and I'm not trying to logic the grief out of you — but I am curious about this idea that love needs to be actively demonstrated to be real. When you think about your mom, do you believe she knew she was loved by you, not just in her final moments, but across the whole of your relationship together?

client: Yeah, I think she knew. We had a complicated relationship at times, but I called her every Sunday without fail, and she used to joke that I was the only one of her kids who actually checked in regularly. But now I'm realizing that admitting she knew I loved her almost makes the loss feel bigger somehow, not smaller, like I'm removing the one excuse I had to keep punishing myself and I'm not sure I'm ready to let that go yet.
therapist: What you just said takes real courage and self-awareness — you've named something so important: that the guilt has been serving a purpose, giving you a way to stay close to her, to keep doing something for her, even if that something is suffering. That's not weakness, that's love looking for somewhere to go when its usual path is gone. I'm wondering, gently — what do you imagine she would actually want for you in these okay moments, if she could tell you herself?

client: She would want me to be okay, I know that without a doubt — she used to worry about me more than anyone else in the family, always asking if I was taking care of myself. But knowing what she'd want and actually letting myself have it feel like two completely different things, and part of me wonders if this is just another reframe that makes sense in theory but won't stick when I'm standing in the grocery store staring at that box of tea. I guess I'm scared that if I stop punishing myself, I'll just feel the emptiness underneath even more, and I don't know if that's better or worse.
therapist: You've just uncovered something really significant — the self-punishment hasn't just been about love, it's also been a shield against the raw emptiness underneath, and in a way, the guilt has been keeping you company in the absence of her. That emptiness you're afraid of is real, and I don't want to pretend that moving toward it will be painless — but I'm struck by the fact that you've been carrying both the grief *and* the weight of punishing yourself, and I wonder if the emptiness on its own might actually be more bearable than you fear. What do you think it would feel like to just let yourself grieve her without also being on trial for it?

client: Honestly, just imagining it makes me feel a strange kind of relief and terror at the same time, like standing at the edge of something I can't see the bottom of. I think it might actually feel quieter, maybe even more honest, but I've been in this pattern for six months and I don't know how you just... stop putting yourself on trial when it's become such a habit. I guess I'm worried that I'll try to let go of the guilt and then feel like I'm failing at that too, like I'll find a way to turn even grieving "correctly" into another thing to be anxious about.
therapist: You've just identified something really important about yourself — that your mind has a well-worn habit of turning things into pass/fail tests, and you're already anticipating that trap, which is actually a sign of real self-awareness rather than a reason to give up before you start. I want to gently suggest that "letting go of guilt" doesn't have to be another goal to achieve or fail at — it might look less like a decision and more like just noticing, moment by moment, when you're putting yourself on trial and offering yourself the tiniest bit of the same compassion you'd give your brother if he were the one standing in that grocery store aisle. I'm curious — what would it look like, just in one small moment this week, to catch that self-punishment happening and simply witness it without joining in?

client: I think the grocery store aisle is actually a good example to work with, because that's probably where it'll happen again, and maybe I could just... notice that I'm spiraling instead of immediately drowning in it. But I'm skeptical about the compassion part, like I understand the concept of treating myself how I'd treat my brother, but in the moment it feels almost foreign, like trying to speak a language I've never actually learned. I guess I could try just noticing, without the pressure of also having to fix how I feel about it — that part at least feels like something I might actually be able to do.
therapist: That reframe you just made on your own — separating "noticing" from "fixing" — is genuinely significant, and it's exactly the right size of step, because self-compassion really is like a language you have to learn gradually, not something that arrives fully formed. Just noticing the spiral in that aisle, without demanding that you also immediately feel better about it, is a real and meaningful act — it's the difference between being swept away by the wave and being able to say "there's a wave." I'm wondering, when you imagine yourself in that moment, pausing to just notice — is there anything you might say to yourself, even something small and imperfect, that feels even slightly more gentle than what your inner critic usually says?

client: Maybe something like... "this makes sense, she was your mom" — just something that acknowledges why it hurts without immediately telling myself I should be over it by now. It feels almost too simple when I say it out loud, and I'm not sure my inner critic is going to just step aside because I've found a nicer phrase to say. But I think that sentence at least feels true, which is different from some affirmation I don't actually believe.
therapist: "This makes sense, she was your mom" is not too simple — it's actually profound, because it's true, and you're right that truth lands differently than a hollow affirmation you're trying to convince yourself of. Your inner critic won't step aside easily, and that's okay — you're not trying to silence it, you're just introducing one true, kind sentence into the conversation it's been having alone for six months. I'm curious — how does it feel to have found those words yourself, rather than having someone hand them to you?

client: It feels a little surprising, honestly, like I came in here not expecting much and somehow ended up finding something that actually feels like mine. I think that matters, because usually when someone tells me how I should feel or what I should say to myself it just slides off, but this came from somewhere real. I'm still not sure one sentence is going to be enough when I'm standing there in that aisle, but I think I'm slightly less afraid of that moment than I was an hour ago.
therapist: What you just described — coming in with low expectations and leaving with something that feels genuinely yours — that's not a small thing, and I want you to really take that in for a moment. You did that work; I just asked the questions, but you found the words, you made the connections, you identified the pattern, and that means you can trust yourself to keep doing that even when I'm not here. And "slightly less afraid" after six months of carrying this alone is not a small shift — so I'm wondering, as you leave today, what feels most important to hold onto from what you discovered?

client: I think the most important thing is that distinction between the guilt and the grief, that they're not the same thing and I don't have to keep carrying both just to prove I loved her. And maybe that sentence — "this makes sense, she was your mom" — as something to come back to, not as a magic fix but just as a small true thing to hold onto when the wave hits. I'm still a little skeptical about how much one session can really shift six months of this, but I think I'm willing to come back and find out, which honestly is more than I expected to feel when I walked in.
therapist: What you're leaving with today is real — that distinction between guilt and grief, and one small true sentence, might seem modest, but you've essentially loosened a knot that's been tightening for six months, and that's not nothing. Your skepticism is welcome here; you don't have to believe this will work in order to keep showing up and finding out, and honestly, the fact that you're willing to come back despite that skepticism tells me something important about your own resilience. I'll look forward to hearing how that moment in the aisle goes — and how it feels to face it carrying a little less than you were before.
